<!-- proposition-1: body_md -->
\label{prop_AI-AP}
    \[ \mathrm{e}_q(z,u)\mathrm{e}_q(-z,v)=1 \] 
    if and only if 
    \[ \mathrm{P}_n(u,v;q)=0, \qquad n\ge 1. \]
<!-- end proposition-1 -->
<!-- proposition-2: body_md -->
\[ \mathrm{P}_{2}(u,v;q) = u+v-(1+q). \]
<!-- end proposition-2 -->
<!-- proposition-3: body_md -->
\[ \mathrm{P}_3(u,v;q) = (u-v) \Bigl( u^2+uv+v^2-(1+q+q^2) \Bigr). \]
<!-- end proposition-3 -->
<!-- proof-1: body_md -->
Direct computation from (\ref{eqn_PolyUV}) gives 
\[ 
    \mathrm{P}_3(u,v;q) = u^3-(1+q+q^2)u+ (1+q+q^2)v-v^3. 
\] 
Factoring yields the result.
<!-- end proof-1 -->
<!-- lemma-1: body_md -->
\label{lemma_geo} 
The simultaneous conditions \[ \mathrm{P}_2(u,v;q)=0, \qquad \mathrm{P}_3(u,v;q)=0 \] define the intersection of the affine line \[ u+v=1+q \] with the cubic variety 
\[ 
(u-v)\Bigl(u^2+uv+v^2-(1+q+q^2)\Bigr)=0. 
\] 
Consequently, every solution belongs to one of the following two branches: \[ u=v, \] or \[ u^2+uv+v^2=1+q+q^2. \]
<!-- end lemma-1 -->
<!-- proof-2: body_md -->
From Proposition 2, 
\[ \mathrm{P}_2(u,v;q)=0 \] 
is equivalent to 
\[ u+v=1+q. \] 
By Proposition 3, 
\[ \mathrm{P}_3(u,v;q)=0 \] 
if and only if 
\[ (u-v) \Bigl( u^2+uv+v^2-(1+q+q^2) \Bigr)=0. \] 
Therefore every common solution of \(\mathrm{P}_2(u,v;q)=\mathrm{P}_3(u,v;q)=0\) must lie on the affine line 
\[ u+v=1+q, \] 
and simultaneously belong to one of the two branches 
\[ u=v, \] 
or 
\[ u^2+uv+v^2=1+q+q^2. \] 
This completes the proof.
<!-- end proof-2 -->
<!-- proposition-4: body_md -->
\label{prop_OCV}
  For every $n\ge0$, \[ \mathrm{P}_{2n+1}(u,u;q)=0. \]
<!-- end proposition-4 -->
<!-- proof-3: body_md -->
From Definition (\ref{eqn_PolyUV}), 
\[ 
\mathrm{P}_{2n+1}(u,u;q) = \sum_{k=0}^{2n+1} (-1)^k \genfrac{[}{]}{0pt}{}{2n+1}{k}_q u^{\binom{2n+1-k}{2}+\binom{k}{2}}. 
\] 
Let 
\[ 
T_k = (-1)^k \genfrac{[}{]}{0pt}{}{2n+1}{k}_q u^{\binom{2n+1-k}{2}+\binom{k}{2}}. 
\] 
Using the symmetry of the $q$-binomial coefficients, 
\[ 
\genfrac{[}{]}{0pt}{}{2n+1}{2n+1-k}_q = \genfrac{[}{]}{0pt}{}{2n+1}{k}_q, 
\] 
we obtain 
\[ T_{2n+1-k} = (-1)^{2n+1-k} \genfrac{[}{]}{0pt}{}{2n+1}{k}_q u^{\binom{k}{2} + \binom{2n+1-k}{2}}=-T_k. 
\] 
The terms cancel pairwise under the involution \[ k\longmapsto 2n+1-k. \] Because \(2n+1\) is odd, there is no fixed point of this involution. Hence every term cancels with a unique partner and 
\[ \mathrm{P}_{2n+1}(u,u;q)=0. \] The proof is complete.
<!-- end proof-3 -->
<!-- lemma-2: body_md -->
\label{lemma_SENS}
Let \(0<q<1\). Then the system \[ 
\mathrm{P}_2(u,u;q)=0, \qquad \mathrm{P}_4(u,u;q)=0 
\] 
has no solution.
<!-- end lemma-2 -->
<!-- proof-4: body_md -->
From \(\mathrm{P}_2(u,u;q)=0\) we obtain 
\[ 
u=\frac{1+q}{2}. 
\] 
Substituting into \(\mathrm{P}_4\) yields 
\[ 
\mathrm{P}_4\!\left(\frac{1+q}{2},\frac{1+q}{2};q\right) = \frac{(1+q)^2}{32} \Bigl( 5+4q+14q^2+4q^3+5q^4 \Bigr). 
\] 
Since all coefficients are positive and \(0<q<1\), the right-hand side is strictly positive. Hence 
\[ \mathrm{P}_4(u,u;q)\neq0. \] 
Therefore, the system has no solution.
<!-- end proof-4 -->
<!-- lemma-3: body_md -->
\label{lemma_SP23}
If \[ \mathrm{P}_2(u,v;q)=P_3(u,v;q)=0 \] and $u\neq v$, then \[ (u,v)=(1,q) \] or \[ (u,v)=(q,1). \]
<!-- end lemma-3 -->
<!-- proof-5: body_md -->
From $\mathrm{P}_2(u,v;q)=0$ we obtain
\[
u+v=1+q.
\]
As $u\neq v$, then from Lemma \ref{lemma_geo}
\[
u^2+uv+v^2=1+q+q^2.
\]
As
\[
u^2+uv+v^2=(u+v)^2-uv,
\]
we obtain
\[
(1+q)^2-uv=1+q+q^2.
\]
Then
\[
uv=q,\qquad u+v=1+q.
\]
Therefore $(u,v)\in\{(1,q),(q,1)\}$.
<!-- end proof-5 -->
<!-- theorem-1: body_md -->
\label{theo_rigidez}
The identity \[ \mathrm{e}_q(z,u)\mathrm{e}_q(-z,v)=1 \] holds if and only if 
\[ (u,v)\in\{(1,q),(q,1)\}. \]
<!-- end theorem-1 -->
<!-- proof-6: body_md -->
By Proposition~\ref{prop_AI-AP}, the identity 
\[ \mathrm{e}_q(z,u)\mathrm{e}_q(-z,v)=1 \] 
is equivalent to the vanishing of all coefficient polynomials 
\[ \mathrm{P}_n(u,v;q), \qquad n\ge1. \] 
In particular, 
\[ \mathrm{P}_2(u,v;q)=\mathrm{P}_3(u,v;q)=0. \] 
By Lemma~\ref{lemma_geo}, every solution belongs either to the symmetric branch \(u=v\) or the nonsymmetric branch \(u\neq v\). Lemma~\ref{lemma_SENS} excludes the symmetric branch. Hence \(u\neq v\). Applying Lemma~\ref{lemma_SP23} yields 
\[ (u,v)=(1,q) \] 
or 
\[ (u,v)=(q,1). \] 
Conversely, the classical Jackson identity 
\[ \mathrm{e}_q(z)\mathrm{E}_q(-z)=1 \] 
implies 
\[ \mathrm{e}_q(z,1)\mathrm{e}_q(-z,q)=1. \] 
Interchanging the two factors gives 
\[ \mathrm{e}_q(z,q)\mathrm{e}_q(-z,1)=1. \] 
Therefore the stated pairs are precisely the solutions of the multiplicative inversion problem.
<!-- end proof-6 -->
